codebook.source: PMLB 'churn' (the telecom customer churn data distributed with MLC++/ the 'churn' example, 5,000 customers); state codes decoded as PMLB's sorted label encoding of the two-letter state abbreviations (checked: the most common code is West Virginia, as in the original data); area codes are the recorded telephone area codes; plans are no = 0, yes = 1 (checked against voice-mail message counts)

sentences.text: This part adds up most inputs with fixed weights: an international plan raises a typical customer's chance of leaving from about 3% to about 31%, and a voice-mail plan lowers it to under 1%.
More voice-mail messages raise it steadily, from about 3% at 0 to about 10% at 32 messages, flattening out near the bottom because the predicted chance cannot go much lower.
A higher evening charge and more international minutes also raise it steadily, each from about 2% to about 4% across their usual range.

Through it, the state moves the chance from about 3% in West Virginia to about 11% in Washington and about 7% in New Jersey, and to under 1% in Hawaii and in Rhode Island (72 to 122 training customers per state).
This part adds up two parts: a rise from 3 customer-service calls upwards and a second rise from 4 calls upwards.
From 3 calls upwards it adds to the chance slowly at first, then faster: for a typical such customer, 4 calls take it from about 3% to about 18%.
Up to 3 calls it barely moves a typical customer's chance, which stays at about 3%, rising slowly at first, then faster.
